title: Aeroflot 1668
summary: The flight departed Olyokminsk at 18:10 in good weather. At 18:24, radar showed the aircraft at 4,500 meters 75 kilometers from Olyokminsk. At 18:28, radar contact was lost. The aircraft was found crashed the next day with both wings and empennage separated from fuselage due to high aerodynamic loads. The aircraft was in an 80 degree nose-down attitude at impact. The exact cause could not be determined but may have involved flight control or structural failure.

title: 1968 Thule Air Base B-52 crash
summary: On January 21, 1968, a United States Air Force Boeing B-52 Stratofortress carrying four B28FI thermonuclear bombs on a Cold War 'Chrome Dome' alert mission experienced a cabin fire that forced the crew to abandon the aircraft over Thule Air Base, Greenland. Six crew members ejected safely, but one crew member without an ejection seat was killed while attempting to bail out. The aircraft crashed on sea ice in North Star Bay, causing the conventional explosives aboard to detonate and the nuclear payload to rupture and disperse, resulting in radioactive contamination of the area. The secondary stage of one nuclear weapon was not recovered after the cleanup operation.
probable_cause: The accident resulted from a cabin fire that forced abandonment of the aircraft. The crew was unable to carry out an emergency landing at Thule Air Base due to the severity of the fire. The crash dispersed radioactive material and led to policy changes, with USAF Strategic Air Command 'Chrome Dome' operations discontinued immediately after the accident.

Expeditions between 2003 and 2024 have recovered remains and wreckage from Himalayan glaciers, confirming the aircraft went down in terrain at about 18,000 ft.

title: Civil Air Transport 10
summary: A Boeing 727-92C registered B-1018 operating Flight 10 from Hong Kong to Taipei crashed into a residential area in Linkou Township, Taipei County on the evening of 16 February 1968. During an instrument landing system approach to Songshan Airport, the aircraft descended below the prescribed glide path. A senior pilot occupied the pilot-in-command seat but was not the designated captain for the flight. This pilot failed to maintain the proper approach altitude, allowing the aircraft to descend below the glide path. When the radio altimeter warning activated at approximately 350 feet, corrective action was not taken in time. The aircraft initially contacted the ground and slid for approximately 200 meters, briefly became airborne again, and then struck trees and a farmhouse. Twenty-one crew and passengers died, along with one person on the ground. Forty-two people were injured.
probable_cause: Pilot error during the ILS approach. The senior pilot occupying the pilot-in-command seat failed to maintain proper approach altitude and did not take corrective action when the radio altimeter warning activated. The aircraft was mechanically sound and weather conditions were not a contributing factor.

title: 1968 Sainte-Marie Douglas DC-6 crash
summary: A Douglas DC-6B military transport aircraft departed Gillot Airport at 23:15 on 9 March 1968. The flight had been brought forward from the following morning due to schedule changes, giving the crew insufficient rest. In bad weather conditions, the crew did not follow standard procedure and made an incorrect turn after takeoff, turning right toward mountains instead of veering left out over the ocean. Approximately five kilometers southeast of the runway, the aircraft crashed into a hill in bad weather and caught fire, killing all 19 people on board including French Army Chief of Staff General Charles Ailleret.

title: Aer Lingus 712

The aircraft was proceeding normally until a call was heard with probable contents twelve thousand feet descending spinning rapidly; thereafter no further radio contact was established. Investigation lasted two years but a definitive cause was never determined. A 2002 review concluded the crash was likely caused by a chain of events starting with flutter-induced fatigue failure of the elevator trim tab mechanism, though other theories including bird strike or structural failure from corrosion were also proposed.

title: Braniff 352
summary: Braniff Flight 352, a Lockheed L-188A Electra, departed Houston for Dallas on May 3, 1968, climbing to 20,000 feet. About 25 minutes into the flight, the crew encountered severe thunderstorm activity with hail. The crew requested and received clearance for a 180-degree right turn to escape the weather. During the turn, the aircraft's bank angle exceeded 90 degrees and the nose pitched down 40 degrees, producing a peak acceleration of 4.3g that exceeded the airframe's ultimate structural strength. The aircraft broke apart in flight, killing all 85 occupants.
probable_cause: The stressing of the aircraft structure beyond its ultimate strength during an attempted recovery from an unusual attitude induced by turbulence associated with a thunderstorm. The operation in the turbulence resulted from a decision to penetrate an area of known severe weather.

The aircraft went into an uncontrolled descent after structural failure occurred.

The fuselage came to rest inverted with the top portion (roof) of the fuselage torn away

title: Pan Am 799
summary: Pan Am Flight 799, a Boeing 707-321C cargo aircraft operated by Pan American World Airways, crashed at Elmendorf Air Force Base near Anchorage during takeoff on December 26, 1968. The aircraft took off with flaps retracted due to cold weather icing prevention procedures, but the takeoff warning system failed to alert the crew because Pan Am had not implemented Boeing Service Bulletin 2384 reducing the warning system throttle actuation point for cold weather. The aircraft stalled immediately after becoming airborne, with the stick shaker vibrating and the right wing striking the ground 59.2 seconds after takeoff.
probable_cause: Takeoff with flaps retracted due to defective checklist design that failed to include flap-lowering reminder in pre-takeoff checklist, combined with inoperative takeoff warning system from non-implementation of Boeing Service Bulletin 2384 for cold weather threshold adjustment

factors.evidence: First Officer Markestein lowered flaps during initial taxi checklist reading but Captain Moen retracted them to prevent icing, and flaps item did not appear in pre-takeoff checklist to remind pilots
lower-flaps item appeared only on the taxi checklist and was not included in the pre-takeoff checklist which comes after the taxi checklist

takeoff warning system should sound audible warning but did not happen because Pan American had failed to implement Boeing January 31 1967 Service Bulletin 2384 recommending warning system throttle actuation point be reduced from 42 degrees to 25 degrees for cold weather conditions
Pan Am operations engineering group had decided that Boeing service bulletin was inapplicable to Pan Am aircraft for reasons they never documented
cockpit stick shaker began to vibrate a safety feature to alert pilots of imminent aerodynamic stall immediately after plane left the ground
aircraft banked to right and right wing touched ground and plane crashed 59.2 seconds after takeoff

events.text: First Officer Markestein advanced engines and aircraft left ground from Runway 23 at Elmendorf Air Force Base
Cockpit stick shaker began to vibrate indicating imminent aerodynamic stall
Boeing 707-321C aircraft banked to the right immediately after becoming airborne
Right wing touched ground and plane crashed 59.2 seconds after takeoff beyond Runway 23 exploding from ground impact

notes: Thorough investigation with clear multi-factor causal chain
Boeing Service Bulletin 2384 non-implementation critical to chain of events
NTSB recommended checklist redesign to prevent similar incidents

title: North Central Airlines 458
summary: During a night approach to O'Hare in 200-foot ceilings and light rain, at 210 feet the CV-580 began climbing. The captain initiated a go-around but the aircraft continued climbing and stalled. It rolled left, struck the ground, and crashed into a hangar. The NTSB determined the captain experienced spatial disorientation from atmospheric refraction of approach lights at a critical moment when transitioning between instrument and visual reference.
probable_cause: Spatial disorientation of the captain caused by atmospheric refraction of approach lights during transition from instrument to visual flight reference, combined with relatively low command experience in the CV-580.

factors.evidence: The aircraft began its approach to O'Hare, which had a 200 ft ceiling with light rain and fog
Spatial disorientation of the captain precipitated by atmospheric refraction of either the approach lights or landing lights at a critical point in the approach
the captain of Flight 458, although experienced, had relatively few hours of experience as the pilot-in-command in CV-580s
Flight 458 lost speed until it stalled 13 seconds after the initiation of the go-around
The aircraft entered a steep left bank, and its left wing struck the ground

events.text: Aircraft at 8:14 p.m. CST began approach to O'Hare with 200 ft ceiling, light rain and fog
At 8:20 p.m. CST, cleared to land on Runway 14R, at 4500 ft from threshold descended to 210 ft
From 210 ft altitude CV-580 began sustained climb for 11 seconds, captain initiated go-around
Aircraft continued to climb, stalled after 13 seconds, entered steep left bank and its left wing struck the ground

title: MacRobertson Miller Airlines 1750
summary: Vickers Viscount Flight 1750 was descending from 19,000 ft to Port Hedland when half the right wing separated in flight at 7,000 ft on descent. Investigation found metal fatigue in the wing spar's lower boom with cracks affecting 85 percent of the cross-section, initiated by improper maintenance of a bush that broached the hole and removed the interference fit. The outer half-wing and engine separated, and the fuselage struck the ground 26 seconds later.
probable_cause: Metal fatigue in the right wing's lower boom caused structural failure and in-flight separation of the outer half-wing. The fatigue was initiated at a bolt hole where improper maintenance actions years earlier had scored the hole and removed the interference fit of a structural bush, reducing fatigue resistance.

factors.evidence: some years before the accident, the bush at the bolt hole had been manipulated with a conical tool causing it to be re-inserted and broach the anodised material, scoring the wall of the hole
metal fatigue had caused cracks to grow across the lower boom until they affected approximately 85% of the cross-sectional area
the lower boom suddenly broke in two and the outer half of the right wing separated from the aircraft in flight
the wing separation led to loss of control and the aircraft fuselage struck the ground

events.text: Flight 1750 took off from Perth Airport at 8:36 am with two pilots, two air hostesses and twenty-two passengers
The pilot advised the aircraft was 30 nautical miles short of destination and passing 7,000 ft on descent to Port Hedland
Four seconds after the last transmission, half of the right wing including the outer engine and propeller separated from the aircraft
Twenty-six seconds after wing separation the aircraft fuselage struck the ground on Indee Station
